items.q: In a news feed, what does 'fanout-on-write' mean?

options.t: The post is pushed into each follower's precomputed feed at post time
options.why: Right. The work happens once, at write time, so every follower's feed read becomes a single cheap cache lookup instead of a merge across hundreds of accounts.

options.t: Building a user's feed from scratch, at read time, every time they open the app
options.why: That's fanout-on-read, also called pull. The 'write' in the name tells you when the work happens — at post time, not at read time.

options.t: Replicating each post to multiple database nodes
options.why: That's replication for durability (Chapter 1.8). Fanout is about distributing a post into follower feeds, not about copies for safety.

options.t: Broadcasting a post to every user of the platform
options.why: Fanout only targets the author's followers. Broadcasting to everyone would be write amplification with no upper bound at all.

items.q: The chapter estimates ~200K feed reads/sec at peak against ~5K posts/sec. What decision does that ratio drive?

options.t: Do extra work at write time so reads become cheap cache hits
options.why: Yes — a ~50:1 read/write ratio is the whole argument for precomputing feeds. You gladly amplify the rare operation (writes) to make the common one (reads) a single lookup.

options.t: Shard the posts database by post ID so writes spread evenly across nodes
options.why: Sharding choices come from data size and access patterns, not directly from this ratio. The ratio's job is deciding where the compute happens: write time vs read time.

options.t: Use a stronger consistency model for reads
options.why: Backwards — heavy read traffic pushes you toward relaxing consistency (cached, slightly stale feeds), not tightening it.

options.t: Add more app servers
options.why: Capacity planning is downstream. The ratio's architectural message is about precomputation — that's the decision the estimate exists to gate.

items.q: What single fact forces the feed to use a hybrid push/pull design instead of pure push?

options.t: Follower counts follow a power law, so one celebrity post means 100M+ writes
options.why: Correct. Push is fine for the average account (~200 followers). It's the tail — accounts with tens or hundreds of millions of followers — that turns one tap into minutes of total fleet capacity.

options.t: Redis cannot store that many lists
options.why: It can — the chapter sizes the whole feed cache at ~2.4 TB across ~40 shards. Storage isn't the blocker; write amplification per celebrity post is.

options.t: Users follow too many accounts on average, which makes every read-time merge expensive
options.why: That's a pull-side cost (more outboxes to merge at read). The hybrid is forced by the write side: a few authors with enormous follower counts.

options.t: Posts contain media that is too large to copy
options.why: Media never enters fanout at all — only post IDs are pushed, and media lives on the CDN. The problem is the number of writes, not their size.

items.q: Why does the feed cache store post IDs rather than full post bodies?

options.t: IDs keep the cache at ~2.4 TB instead of hundreds, and bodies are cached once and shared
options.why: Right. A post pushed to 200 followers as a body would be stored 200 times; as an ID it's 16 bytes per follower plus one shared cached body. The cost is a hydration step at read, which the post cache makes cheap.

options.t: Redis cannot store objects larger than 1 KB
options.why: Redis handles values up to hundreds of MB. The reason is economics and duplication, not a technical limit.

options.t: Post bodies change too frequently to cache safely, so only stable identifiers can be stored
options.why: Nearly the opposite — post bodies are essentially immutable, which makes them ideal cache material. That's exactly why one shared post cache works so well.

options.t: IDs are needed for the ranking model to work
options.why: The ranker works on candidates either way; it fetches its own features. The ID-only choice is about RAM and write amplification.

items.q: The scorer service misses its 50 ms latency budget on a request. What does the feed service do?

options.t: Sort the candidates chronologically and serve that
options.why: Yes — the degradation-menu move (Chapter 2.7). The user gets a slightly dumber feed instead of an error or a slow page, and chrono_served_rate records that it happened.

options.t: Return an error and let the client retry
options.why: That turns a quality problem into an availability problem. The feed's contract is availability first; there's always a servable feed without the model.

options.t: Wait for the scorer — ranking is a hard requirement
options.why: Blocking blows the 200 ms page budget for something users can live without for one request. Ranking is valuable, not load-bearing.

options.t: Serve the previous session's cached page again
options.why: Serving stale identical content on refresh looks broken to the user. Fresh candidates in time order is strictly better and just as cheap.

items.q: What consistency contract do like counts have in this design?

options.t: Approximate now, exact eventually — increments aggregate asynchronously and reconcile later
options.why: Right. A billion likes a day can't be synchronous updates on hot post rows. Sharded counters absorb the storm, cached reads lag by seconds, and a reconciliation job repairs drift from the durable event log.

options.t: Strongly consistent — every like blocks until the counter is updated, so counts are always exact
options.why: Exact real-time counts on a viral post would mean millions of serialized writes on one row. Nobody can fact-check '1.2M likes' anyway — the display rounding hides more than the lag does.

options.t: Counts are computed fresh from the likes table on every read
options.why: A COUNT(*) per post per feed read at 200K reads/sec is astronomically expensive. Counts are precomputed and cached, like the feed itself.

options.t: Counts are only updated once per day
options.why: Too stale — counts converge within seconds to minutes. Eventual consistency here means a short, bounded lag, not a nightly batch.

items.q: Why does offset pagination ('give me items 26–50') break for a ranked feed?

options.t: The ranked order shifts between requests, so fixed offsets overlap or skip items
options.why: Exactly. New posts arrive and scores change between page one and page two. The fix is a session snapshot: freeze the ranked ID list once, then page through the frozen copy by cursor.

options.t: Offsets are too slow for Redis lists
options.why: Redis list index reads are fast. The problem is correctness — a moving ranking under fixed offsets — not performance.

options.t: The feed has too many items to number
options.why: A feed page numbers a few hundred candidates at most. Scale isn't the issue; the reshuffling between requests is.

options.t: Clients cannot store an offset between requests, so the server would have to track it for them
options.why: Clients store cursors fine — that's the mechanism. The issue is what the offset points into when the underlying order won't hold still.

items.q: The fanout queue develops a 30-minute backlog. What happens to the posts inside it?

options.t: They arrive in followers' feeds late — nothing is lost, the post was durable before the 201
options.why: Right. Durability was settled at write time in the posts DB; the queue is durable too. Fanout lag delays delivery, never destroys it — 'delayed, not lost' is the exact phrase to say in the interview.

options.t: Posts older than the queue's retention window are silently dropped once the backlog grows past it
options.why: Even if a queue aged out events, the posts themselves live in the posts DB and reach readers via the pull path. The design has no point where an accepted post can vanish.

options.t: Users must repost anything that didn't fan out
options.why: Never — the 201 was a promise. Asking users to redo accepted writes means the system broke its durability contract.

options.t: The feed switches to chronological mode
options.why: Chrono fallback is the scorer's failure mode, not fanout's. A fanout backlog just means feed lists update late.

items.q: Meta's 'Product Architecture' flavor of this question grades something the pure systems round mostly doesn't. What?

options.t: The API contract and client behavior — payload shape, cursor semantics, optimistic UI
options.why: Yes. Product Architecture wants hydrated payloads that paint in one pass, opaque cursors, optimistic like counts, cached-then-refresh rendering — the seam between backend and app is the graded surface.

options.t: Deeper knowledge of ML ranking models
options.why: Neither round expects model internals — treating the scorer as a budgeted service with a fallback is the expected depth in both.

options.t: Ability to write production code on the whiteboard
options.why: That's the coding rounds. Product Architecture is still a design interview; it just centers the product-facing contract.

options.t: Database schema normalization
options.why: Schema basics are table stakes everywhere. The distinctive graded surface is the client-visible API and app behavior.

items.q: An account with 3 million followers publishes a post. Trace what happens in this chapter's design.

options.t: The post lands in the posts DB (the author's outbox); fanout skips it; followers' read paths merge it in from the outbox
options.why: Correct — 3M is over the 1M threshold, so no pushes happen at all. The outbox write already occurred as part of storing the post, and readers stitch it in at read time from a heavily cached key.

options.t: Fanout pushes to all 3M followers but at lower priority
options.why: Priority tiers still spend 3M writes per post. The hybrid's point is that above the threshold you spend zero fanout writes, because read-time merging is cheaper.

options.t: The post is pushed only to the most active 1M followers
options.why: Partial fanout gives you both code paths' costs on the same post and still needs the merge for everyone else. The clean split — push or pull per author — is simpler and sufficient.

options.t: The post goes into a lower-priority celebrity queue that fans out to all 3M followers overnight, when spare write capacity is free
options.why: Overnight delivery breaks the freshness requirement badly for exactly the posts most people are waiting to see. Read-time merge delivers them within seconds with no fanout at all.

items.q: During hydration, the counter service times out but the post cache and CDN respond. What should the feed service return?

options.t: The full page, with stale or omitted counts on affected posts
options.why: Right — per-field graceful degradation. Counts are decoration; the page is the product. Holding 25 rendered posts hostage for a like number inverts the value of what you're serving.

options.t: An error, since the response would be incomplete
options.why: Failing a whole page over its least important field turns a minor dependency wobble into user-visible downtime. The parallel-hydration design exists precisely so fields can fail independently.

options.t: Only the posts whose counts loaded successfully
options.why: Dropping posts because a side-dish fetch failed shrinks and reshuffles the feed unpredictably — far more visible than a missing count.

options.t: Retry the counts until they arrive
options.why: Retrying inside the request burns the 200 ms budget on the field users check least. Ship now; the next refresh will have fresh counts.

items.q: A user who has been inactive for 90 days opens the app. Their feed list was evicted. What happens?

options.t: The read falls back to pull: fetch followees' outboxes, merge, rank, serve, and rebuild the cache in the background
options.why: Yes — one slower first page, then back on the fast path. The pull path doubles as cache-miss recovery, new-user backfill, and dormant-return handling: one mechanism, several problems.

options.t: They see an empty feed until new posts are fanned out to them
options.why: Fanout only covers the future; an empty feed for a returning user would look like a broken app. The posts DB has everything needed to rebuild the past on demand.

options.t: A batch job pre-rebuilds all inactive users' feeds nightly
options.why: That re-creates the exact waste the dormant-skip optimization removed — building feeds for people who may never return. Rebuild lazily, on the read that proves they're back.

options.t: The app shows generic trending content until a background job re-fans-out their followees' recent posts into a fresh list
options.why: Trending fallback is for users who follow nobody. This user has a follow graph; the pull path serves their real feed on the very first request.

items.q: Why does the fanout worker skip followers who haven't opened the app in 30 days?

options.t: Those writes land in lists nobody reads, and dormant users rebuild by pull if they return
options.why: Right — it can cut fanout cost dramatically, and the pull path guarantees correctness for anyone who comes back. Classic trade: cheaper steady-state writes for one slower page on return.

options.t: Inactive users' Redis lists have already been evicted, so the fanout write would fail with an error
options.why: Writes to a fresh key would simply recreate the list — Redis doesn't error. The point is that the write is wasted, not that it fails.

options.t: It protects those users' privacy
options.why: Privacy isn't involved — the post is public to followers either way. This is purely a cost optimization on write amplification.

options.t: To keep the follower list query fast
options.why: The graph query returns everyone regardless; filtering happens after. The savings are in the Redis writes not performed, which dwarf the query cost.

items.q: Feed quality has quietly degraded for a week: engagement is down, but every latency and error dashboard is green. Which failure fits?

options.t: The feature pipeline is lagging — the scorer is ranking confidently on stale features
options.why: This is the silent failure the chapter flags: stale affinity data doesn't error, it just ranks worse. It's why feature age gets monitored with the same seriousness as latency.

options.t: The scorer service is down, so the feed has silently fallen back to chronological order
options.why: A dead scorer is loud — chrono_served_rate pins to 1.0 and its own error metrics fire. The scenario says everything is green, which points at a failure no standard dashboard catches.

options.t: The fanout queue has a backlog
options.why: Backlog shows up immediately in the fanout-lag metric and in 'my followers see my posts late' complaints — loud in a different way, and it doesn't smell like a slow week-long quality drift.

options.t: The feed cache hit rate dropped
options.why: Hit-rate drops surface as latency (pull rebuilds are slower) — which the scenario rules out. Quality-down-while-green is the signature of stale ranking inputs.

items.q: Users report seeing the same post twice: once yesterday evening, again this morning. Which mechanism failed?

options.t: The seen store — the cross-session filter that drops already-served post IDs during candidate generation
options.why: Right. Within one session the frozen snapshot prevents duplicates; across sessions it's the seen store's job. Yesterday-then-today duplication is precisely its failure signature (expired too early, or the filter was skipped).

options.t: The session-snapshot cursor
options.why: The snapshot only guards one session's pages against each other. These sightings are in different sessions — outside the snapshot's jurisdiction entirely.

options.t: The ranking model re-scored the post highly
options.why: The scorer may indeed love the post both days — that's allowed. The seen filter exists to overrule it for content the user already saw; scoring it isn't the bug, serving it is.

options.t: Fanout delivered the post twice — the same post ID was written into this user's feed list on two different days
options.why: Duplicate IDs in a feed list are expected under at-least-once delivery — and are exactly what read-time dedup and the seen filter are there to absorb. The read-side filter failing is the story.

items.q: A user taps like and instantly sees the count go from 41 to 42, even though the counter service won't process the increment for seconds. How?

options.t: The client bumps the displayed count optimistically; the backend converges later
options.why: Yes — read-your-own-writes, faked at the edge. The one number a user actually verifies is their own action, so the client handles it locally while the counter service stays eventually consistent for everyone else.

options.t: Like writes are synchronous even though reads are cached
options.why: Making every like a synchronous counter write reintroduces the hot-row problem the counter service exists to avoid. The instant '42' never came from the server.

options.t: The counter service prioritizes the liker's read
options.why: Per-user read priority in a shared counter cache would be complex and still racy. Far simpler: the client already knows the user liked it — no server round trip needed to display that.

options.t: Counts are stored per-client, not centrally
options.why: Counts are global facts stored centrally; only the +1 for your own fresh like is layered on locally until the backend catches up.

items.q: At 10x today's traffic, which cost grows fastest and what is the named lever against it?

options.t: The scorer fleet — and the lever is scoring fewer candidates per request
options.why: Right. Fanout and caches scale linearly with cheap operations, but ML inference is expensive per item: 10x requests × 500 candidates is the money pit. Cutting candidates 500 → 200 more than halves it for a measurable quality cost.

options.t: The posts database — the lever is a bigger primary
options.why: Posts are sharded by author and write-light relative to everything else. Vertical scaling is also the weakest lever in the book at this scale.

options.t: The CDN — the lever is more origin servers
options.why: CDNs are built to scale reads almost arbitrarily and offload origins; media is the least worried box in the 10x story.

options.t: The social graph — the lever is caching follower counts
options.why: Follower-count caching is already assumed and trivially cheap. The graph reads scale linearly; nothing about them is the fastest-growing bill.

items.q: Why do media bytes never flow through the feed service — only CDN URLs in the payload?

options.t: Serving images through app servers would drown them in bandwidth that a CDN handles at the edge for a fraction of the cost
options.why: Right (Chapter 1.7). Feed servers do orchestration measured in kilobytes; a single photo can outweigh the entire rest of the page. Clients fetch media directly from edge caches near them.

options.t: The feed service is not allowed to access blob storage
options.why: It could — that's a permissions detail, not the reason. The reason is economics and latency: bytes should travel the short edge path, not through your orchestration tier.

options.t: CDN URLs are needed for the ranking model's media features
options.why: The model uses media *type* as a feature, which comes from post metadata. URL-vs-bytes in the response payload has nothing to do with ranking.

options.t: Media is too large to fit in a JSON response
options.why: Base64-in-JSON is possible, just terrible. The design reason is offloading delivery to the edge, not a format limit.

items.q: Interviewer: 'Push or pull for the feed?' Which answer performs at E5?

options.t: "Hybrid, and the follower distribution decides the split: push under ~1M followers because fanout finishes in seconds, pull above it because one celebrity post is 100M writes — and users follow few enough celebrities that the read merge stays cheap."
options.why: A commitment, driven by the distribution, with both cost curves named and a bounded read-side cost. This is the crux answered as an owner, in three sentences.

options.t: "Push has fast reads but expensive writes; pull has cheap writes but slow reads. Twitter, Instagram and Facebook have each used both at different points, so it really depends on the workload and what the team wants to operate — I could sketch either one."
options.why: True, balanced, and uncommitted — the option-listing pattern. The workload was given to you; 'it depends' after the numbers exist reads as declining to decide.

options.t: "Push, because reads dominate 50:1 and precomputation makes them O(1)."
options.why: Committed and correctly reasoned — for the average case. It walks straight into the celebrity trap the question was built around, which the interviewer will spring one sentence later. Half the distribution isn't the distribution.

options.t: "Pull, because it's always correct and much simpler — no fanout infrastructure to operate."
options.why: The simplicity instinct is healthy, but the numbers kill it here: 200K reads/sec × hundreds of followed accounts is ~80M outbox reads/sec of largely repeated work. Simplicity that ignores the load math reads junior, not lazy-smart.

items.q: You have 20 minutes of deep-dive time left on this problem. Where does a senior candidate spend it?

options.t: The fanout decision and its threshold, then ranking's budget-and-fallback — announced as an agenda
options.why: Fanout is the crux this question exists to probe, and ranking is Meta's favorite follow-up; proposing that agenda out loud is the driving-the-room behavior the rubric rewards.

options.t: The follows table schema and its indexes
options.why: Necessary, routine, and already sketched in five minutes. Spending deep-dive time on assumed competence is touring rooms that aren't on fire.

options.t: A complete multi-region active-active strategy for the feed
options.why: Genuinely deep but not this question's fire — and starting it with 20 minutes left risks the classic unfinished-deep-dive fail. Mention it as an extension; spend the time on the crux.

options.t: Covering every remaining component briefly so nothing is missed
options.why: Breadth was the first half of the interview. The deep-dive phase grades depth on the hard parts; even coverage of easy parts adds no signal at the senior bar.

items.q: The ranking team ships a model that lifts engagement 2% but doubles scorer p99 from 50 ms to 100 ms, blowing your 200 ms page budget on slow requests. Your call as the feed owner?

options.t: Hold the rollout at its current cohort; offer paths that buy the quality inside the budget — fewer scored candidates, a distilled model, or a raised timeout with chrono fallback absorbing the overruns — and let guardrail metrics arbitrate
options.why: This treats latency as a budget you own, not a preference — and negotiates with options rather than vetoing. Naming the fallback as a release valve and letting measurements decide is the operator's answer.

options.t: Ship it — 2% engagement at Meta scale is enormous and worth some latency
options.why: It might be! But 'worth it' isn't yours to declare by vibes when the page SLO breaks — feed latency has its own engagement cost, which this answer never weighs. Unmeasured trade-offs read junior at any level.

options.t: Block it — the 50 ms budget is the contract, full stop
options.why: Budget-as-religion ignores that budgets serve the product. A flat veto with no path forward is the mirror image of shipping blind: a decision without the trade-off examined.

options.t: Ship it and remove the chrono fallback so all feeds get the better model
options.why: Removing the degradation path while doubling the dependency's latency is maximizing exposure at the worst moment. The fallback is what makes bolder model experiments safe at all.

items.q: Interviewer: 'A celebrity with 200M followers posts, and simultaneously your fanout fleet loses half its workers. What actually degrades?' The best answer:

options.t: "Almost nothing couples: the celebrity post skips fanout entirely, so it's live within seconds via read-time merge. The worker loss halves fanout throughput, so ordinary posts arrive late — fanout lag climbs, nothing is lost, and I'd shed dormant-follower pushes to recover."
options.why: This answer shows the design's decoupling paying off under a compound failure, names the user-visible symptom precisely, and includes the recovery lever. Calm, specific, mechanical — the senior register.

options.t: "The celebrity post would be severely delayed since fanout capacity is halved."
options.why: This reveals a missed mechanism: celebrity posts never touch fanout in the hybrid — that's the entire point of the threshold. The failure affects exactly the posts that *do* fan out.

options.t: "Feeds would start erroring until workers are restored."
options.why: The read path doesn't depend on fanout workers at all — it reads caches and outboxes. Confusing write-side degradation with read-side availability misreads the architecture's main seam.

options.t: "We'd need to fail over to the pull path for all users temporarily."
options.why: A global mode-switch is a dramatic intervention the design doesn't need — feed lists still serve reads fine; they're just briefly staler. Overreacting to a lag with a failover reads as not trusting your own architecture.

items.q: A PM demands exact, real-time like counts: 'users deserve accurate numbers.' Your senior response?

options.t: Quantify the cost and probe the need: exact-real-time means serialized writes on viral hot rows for a difference display rounding already hides — then confirm the one case users verify, their own like, is already instant via the optimistic client
options.why: This reframes a feelings-requirement into a cost/benefit the PM can actually decide on, and shows the user-facing need is already met by a cheaper mechanism. Pushing back with numbers and an alternative is the senior pattern.

options.t: Build it — requirements come from product, and engineering's job is to deliver them
options.why: Deference isn't collaboration. Accepting an implicit architectural rewrite (hot-row serialization at a billion likes/day) without surfacing its cost fails the PM as much as the system.

options.t: Refuse — eventual consistency is the industry standard for counters
options.why: 'Industry standard' is an appeal to authority, not an argument. The PM deserves the actual trade-off: what exactness costs here and what approximation actually loses (nearly nothing, post-rounding).

options.t: Compromise by making counts exact for posts under 1,000 likes
options.why: Clever-sounding, but small counts are where the async counter is already accurate within seconds — the compromise spends complexity where the problem doesn't exist and leaves the hot-row case unsolved.

items.q: Interviewer: 'Your 1M threshold — why not 100K, or 10M?' What is this question actually grading?

options.t: Whether the number connects to fanout time, exempted-account population, and read-merge cost — any value whose curves you can defend passes
options.why: Threshold questions are never about the constant; they're calibration probes. Knowing that 100K trades more merging for less write amplification — and what data would move you — is the passing answer at any specific number.

options.t: Whether you know the industry-standard threshold
options.why: There isn't one — real systems tune it continuously against their own distributions. Citing a 'standard' signals memorization where judgment was requested.

options.t: Whether you'll defend your first answer under pressure instead of caving the moment the interviewer pushes back on the number you picked
options.why: Stubbornness isn't conviction. Updating the threshold when the interviewer supplies new constraints is fine — what's graded is whether the reasoning machinery exists, not whether the number survives.

options.t: Whether you can compute 1M × 20 bytes quickly
options.why: Arithmetic is assumed. The probe is about the three cost curves crossing, not the multiplication — a fast wrong-framework answer scores below a slow right-framework one.

items.q: You get to keep exactly three feed alerts. Which set best covers the failure space?

options.t: Feed p99 latency, fanout lag, and chrono_served_rate
options.why: One alert per independent failure domain: the read path's SLO, the write path's health, and the ranking dependency's degradation — together they catch cache trouble (as latency), backlog, and scorer decay. Coverage per alert is the game.

options.t: CPU, memory, and disk on the feed servers
options.why: Resource metrics are causes, not symptoms — they page you for things users may never feel and sleep through things users do feel. Alert on user-visible behavior; keep resources on dashboards.

options.t: Feed p99, feed p50, and feed error rate
options.why: Three views of one failure domain — the read path — while fanout could silently fall a day behind. Redundant coverage of one seam is the classic alerting mistake.

options.t: Scorer p99, feature age, and model engagement lift
options.why: All ranking, no feed. This is the scorer team's page, not the feed owner's — with these three, a dead Redis fleet or a stuck fanout queue pages nobody.
